mula_devanagari: प्रकृतिं पुरुषं चैव विद्ध्य् अनादी उभाव् अपि | विकारांश् च गुणांश् चैव विद्धि प्रकृति-संभवान्
mula_iast: prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ caiva viddhy anādī ubhāv api | vikārāṃś ca guṇāṃś caiva viddhi prakṛti-saṃbhavān
madhva_bhashya: ।।13.20।।यतश्च यत् [13।4] इति वक्तुं प्रकृतिविकारपुरुषान् सङ्क्षिप्याऽऽह। गुणाः सत्त्वादयः। तेषामत्यल्पो विशेषो लयात्सर्ग इति विकाराः पृथगुक्ताः। कार्याकार्यगुणास्तिस्रो यतः स्वल्पोद्भवो जनौ इति माधुच्छन्दसशाखायाम्।
jayatirtha_prameyadipika: ।।13.20।।ननुप्रकृतिं पुरुषं चैव विद्धि इत्यादिकमप्रतिज्ञातं किमित्युच्यते मैवम्।यादृक्च [13।4] इति प्रतिज्ञातस्य सप्रकारस्य क्षेत्रस्य कथनात् तत्प्रतिज्ञाक्रमेण प्रागेव कुतो नोक्तं इत्यत आह -- यतश्चे ति।यतश्च यत् [13।4] इति प्रतिज्ञातं प्रेरकस्वरूपं तावत्प्रभावानन्तरं वक्तव्यं प्राप्तम्। तत्र प्रेरकस्य स्वरूपनिरूपणं प्रेर्यज्ञानमपेक्षते। प्रेर्यं च सप्रकारं क्षेत्रम्? प्रेरकस्वरूपं वक्तुं अनेन प्रेरणीयं सप्रकारं क्षेत्रमुच्यते। तस्य प्रागपि वचने,गौरवं स्यादिति भावः। तर्हि प्रकृतीत्यादि कथमुच्यते ईश्वरातिरिक्तः सर्वोऽपि चेतनाचेतनवर्गः क्षेत्रमित्युच्यते। तत्र प्रकृतिशब्देनमहाभूतानि [13।6] इत्यादिनोक्तानि चतुर्विंशतितत्त्वानि गृह्यन्ते। विकारशब्देनेच्छाद्युपलक्षिताः क्षेत्रान्तर्भूता अपि गुणत्रयाद्याः सर्वे विकारा विवक्षाविशेषवशेन पृथगुपात्ताः। पुरुषशब्देन जीव इति।यावत्सञ्जायते [13।27] इत्यादिना पुनर्वक्ष्यमाणत्वात्पुनरुक्तिदोषं परिहर्तुं संङ्क्षिप्येत्युक्तम्। आह सप्रकारान्निरूपयति। गुणाः सुखदुःखमोहा इति [शं.] कश्चित्। कार्यकारणलक्षणा इत्यन्वयः? तदुभयं निराकर्तुं व्याचष्टे -- गुणा इति। ननु सत्वरजस्तमसामपि प्रकृतिविकारत्वात्विकारांश्च गुणांश्च इति। पृथगुक्तिः किमर्था इत्यत आह -- तेषामि ति। इति ज्ञापयितुमिति शेषः। विकाराः पृथगुक्ता इति विकाराश्च गुणाश्च पृथगुक्ता इत्यर्थः। कार्याश्च तेऽकार्याश्च। तिखस्त्रयः। अनेन सुखाद्यङ्गीकारे विकारेभ्यः पृथग्ग्रहणमयुक्तमित्यपि सूचितम्।

current_dvaita_rendering.english: To explain 'from what, what arises' (13.4), the Lord sums up prakṛti (matter), its vikāra (products) and puruṣa (the conscious being). The guṇa are sattva (clarity) and the rest; the vikāra are named separately because they are only a very slight particularization of the guṇa, arising as creation out of dissolution, as the Mādhucchandasa recension says.
current_dvaita_rendering.divergence_note: THIN: Madhva's supplied comment (source 13.20) is three sentences and does not gloss anādi or say who the puruṣa is here; it only frames the verse as answering 13.4 and explains why vikāra are listed apart from guṇa (slight difference, laya to sarga), citing a Mādhucchandasa text. Rendering kept to what is there; no Dvaita reading of the jīva-Īśvara relation is supplied for this verse.

current_dvaita_everyday: Madhva's note is a reminder to keep categories clean: the basic qualities of a situation and the specific products they turn into are almost the same, but not identical, and worth naming separately. A doctor separating a patient's general constitution from the particular symptom it has produced is doing exactly this.

other_schools_english.advaita: Know prakṛti (matter-nature) and puruṣa (the conscious principle) as the two prakṛti of Īśvara (the Lord), both anādi (without beginning): since the Lord is eternal, His two natures must be eternal too, and to possess these two is precisely what makes Him Lord. Those who split anādī as 'not the first' so as to keep the Lord as sole cause are wrong, for before the two arose there would be nothing to rule, and saṃsāra (the round of birth), bondage and release would become causeless and scripture pointless. Know the vikāra (modifications), from buddhi (intellect) down to body and senses, and the guṇa (qualities) that turn into pleasure, pain and delusion, as born of prakṛti, which is the Lord's triguṇa māyā (three-stranded power of manifestation).
other_schools_english.viśiṣṭādvaita: Know that prakṛti (matter) and puruṣa (the self), mutually conjoined, are both anādi (beginningless). And know that both the vikāra (modifications) such as desire and aversion, which cause bondage, and the guṇa (qualities) such as amānitva (freedom from pride) and the rest, which cause release, are born of prakṛti. This same prakṛti, joined to the self from time without beginning and transformed into the form of the kṣetra (field, the body), binds the self through desire and aversion, and that very prakṛti, through humility and the other virtues, becomes the cause of its apavarga (liberation).
other_schools_english.śuddhādvaita: This is the Bhagavat's own sāṅkhya (enumeration of principles), not that of the sāṅkhya partisans for whom prakṛti is an eternal second beside the self: here prakṛti is the Lord's śakti (power), in two forms, as effect the upādhi (limiting adjunct) of the jīva (individual self) bound with avidyā (ignorance), and as cause the māyā of the paramātman (supreme self); likewise puruṣa is the aṃśin (whole), the root person, and the jīva are His aṃśa (portions). By līlā (play), by His own will, He took up prakṛti; know both as My aṃśa, sat-cit (being-consciousness) in nature, anādi because not other than their cause. Know the vikāra, desire and aversion that bind, and the guṇa, humility and the rest, or sattva and the rest, that lead to amṛta (immortality), as born of prakṛti.
other_schools_english.bhakti: With this verse and the next four the Lord expounds 'what its modifications are and from what it comes, who he is and what his power', by declaring prakṛti and puruṣa the causes of saṃsāra (the round of birth). Know both as anādi (beginningless), for if they had a beginning, another prakṛti would be needed for them, and so without end; prakṛti is beginningless as the śakti (power) of the beginningless Īśvara, and puruṣa is beginningless as His aṃśa (portion), a point Śaṅkara has argued at length, so I do not expand it. Know the vikāra, body, senses and the rest, and the guṇa, their transformations as pleasure, pain and delusion, as sprung from prakṛti.
other_schools_english.advaita-bhakti: In the seventh chapter the Lord set out His two prakṛti, the lower, which is the kṣetra (field), and the higher, which is the jīva (living being); here the lower is called prakṛti, the three-stranded māyā, the power of the Supreme Lord, and the higher is called puruṣa, so there is no contradiction. Know both as anādi (without a cause): prakṛti because it is the cause of the whole world and to seek a cause for it would be endless regress; puruṣa because the joy, grief and fear of every newborn are driven by its past dharma and adharma (merit and demerit), else one would suffer the unearned and lose the earned. Know the vikāra, the sixteen (five great elements and eleven senses), and the guṇa, sattva, rajas and tamas as pleasure, pain and delusion, as having prakṛti alone for their cause.
